title: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court
author: Mark Twain
written: 1885-89, in the years Twain was pouring his fortune into a typesetting machine that never worked
setting: Warwick Castle in the present, and from the second chapter the Britain of 528, from Camelot and the Valley of Holiness to a slave gang on the road and a cave ringed with electrified fence
lengthNote: Forty-four chapters and a frame, about 119,000 words, ending in a postscript written by somebody else
openingLine: It was in Warwick Castle that I came across the curious stranger whom I am going to talk about.
summary: A factory superintendent from Hartford is hit on the head and wakes in Britain in 528. He saves himself with an eclipse, takes the country over as the Boss, and sets about installing the nineteenth century: patent office, schools, newspapers, telephone wires strung through the forest. The first half is a comedy about medieval nonsense meeting American know-how. The second half is about what the Boss does when the country will not keep the improvements, and it ends with twenty-five thousand dead men and the man who killed them unable to get out of the cave.
referenceStyle: chapter number, following the 1889 first edition

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court (eBook 86)
sourceText.note: The 1889 American first edition, with Twain’s spellings and the frame narrator’s preface. The novel’s Britain is the one Malory describes, and the Boss quotes him.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Begun as a notebook joke about a knight in armour with no way to scratch himself, and finished as something much darker.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: Published by Charles L. Webster & Co. with 220 illustrations by Dan Beard, whose politics Twain said were sharper than his own.

atAGlance.label: Source
atAGlance.note: Twain was given Le Morte d'Arthur in 1884 and used it as the quarry for the sixth century throughout.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: A manuscript handed over at Warwick, read overnight, and closed by a postscript in another hand.

structure.label: A Word of Explanation, Chapters I-II
structure.title: Warwick Castle, a blow on the head, and a girl who is not surprised
structure.summary: A tourist at Warwick meets a stranger who talks about the sixth century as though he has been there, and is handed a manuscript on palimpsest to read overnight. The story inside begins in a Hartford arms factory and continues under an oak tree in 528, where a man in armour rides up and a child stares at the stranger's clothes rather than at his.

scenes.title: The stranger at Warwick
scenes.summary: The frame narrator meets the man, hears about bullet-holes in chain mail, and is given the manuscript.

scenes.title: Camelot
scenes.summary: Hank Morgan wakes in open country, is taken prisoner by Sir Kay, and assumes he is in an asylum.

scenes.title: The Yankee's history
scenes.summary: Hartford, the arms factory, and a man who can make anything and invent the machine that makes it.

structure.label: Chapters III-VIII
structure.title: The eclipse, and a new job
structure.summary: At the Round Table the knights tell Malory's stories at length while Hank works out what year it is. Sentenced to burn, he remembers a total eclipse due on the 21st of June, 528, and announces that he will put out the sun. The court buys it, the king makes him perpetual minister, and the nation gives him a title that fits an American better than a duke's would.

scenes.title: Knights of the Table Round
scenes.summary: Their talk is lifted from Malory, and Hank listens to it as a man listens to people who lie without knowing they are lying.

scenes.title: The eclipse
scenes.summary: A threat delivered in a voice charged with doom, timed to an astronomical event, and believed absolutely.

scenes.title: Merlin's tower
scenes.summary: Blowing it up with blasting powder and a lightning rod, to settle which magician the country is going to believe.

scenes.title: The Boss
scenes.summary: Second only to the king, and called by a name nobody in the sixth century had a use for.

structure.label: Chapters IX-XVII
structure.title: Patent office, schools, wires in the woods
structure.summary: Hank builds a modern state underground and out of sight: a teacher factory, a West Point, a newspaper, telephone lines strung at night, soap and matches and stove polish. It is funny, and it is being done by one man with no successor, in a country that has not asked for any of it. The chapters keep the joke going while laying out exactly why it will fail.

scenes.title: The tournament
scenes.summary: A weekly institution the Boss studies the way a manager studies a market.

scenes.title: Beginnings of civilization
scenes.summary: The patent office first, then schools, then the rest — his stated order of priorities.

scenes.title: Freemen
scenes.summary: Hank talks economics to men who cannot see their own position, and loses the argument by winning it.

scenes.title: A royal banquet
scenes.summary: The court at its ease, with the gap between its manners and its cruelty on full display.

structure.label: Chapters XI-XXXVIII
structure.title: Sandy, the king in disguise, and the slave gang
structure.summary: The middle of the novel takes the Boss out of his workshop and into the country. He rescues princesses who turn out to be pigs, empties Morgan le Fay's dungeons, crawls into a smallpox hut, and travels in peasant clothes with a king who cannot learn to walk like one. The comedy thins as they go; by the slave gang it has gone, and the book's opinion of the sixth century has become an opinion about the nineteenth.

scenes.title: Slow torture
scenes.summary: Armour in the sun, with an insect inside it and no way to reach it — the joke the whole novel grew out of.

scenes.title: Morgan le Fay
scenes.summary: A charming hostess who stabs a page for brushing her knee, and whose dungeons hold men who have forgotten why they are there.

scenes.title: The holy fountain
scenes.summary: A miracle performed with a pump, fire-works and two assistants, and received as one.

scenes.title: A pitiful incident
scenes.summary: The king and the Boss are sold as slaves, and the rescue arrives on bicycles.

structure.label: Chapters XXXIX-XLIV
structure.title: The republic, the Interdict, and the cave
structure.summary: Hank unhorses the flower of chivalry with a lasso and then a revolver, proclaims a republic when Arthur dies, and finds the Church has turned the country against him with an interdict. Fifty-two boys and one engineer meet the assembled knighthood behind electric fences and Gatling guns. The Boss wins in an afternoon, is trapped by the dead he has made, and the manuscript ends in somebody else's handwriting.

scenes.title: The Yankee's fight with the knights
scenes.summary: A lasso, then a revolver, and the end of tournaments.

scenes.title: War!
scenes.summary: Arthur dead, the republic declared, and the whole of England on the other side.

scenes.title: The battle of the sand-belt
scenes.summary: Twenty-five thousand men killed by wire, water and machine guns in a single engagement, described in the flat voice of an engineer.

scenes.title: A postscript by Clarence
scenes.summary: The Boss is put to sleep by Merlin for thirteen centuries, and a boy finishes the book for him.

characters.name: Hank Morgan
characters.role: The Boss: arms-factory superintendent, and perpetual minister to King Arthur
characters.summary: Practical, funny, humane in his opinions and dangerous in his methods. He can make anything, and the novel's argument is that a man who can make anything will eventually make the thing that settles the argument for him. He never doubts that he is on the side of progress, including on the last afternoon.
characters.clue: Stops an execution with an eclipse, and ends by counting the dead as an engineering result.

characters.name: Clarence
characters.role: A page at Camelot, then the Boss's chief of staff
characters.summary: Picked up in the first chapters as a cheerful boy and turned into the one person who understands the whole operation. He runs the newspaper, the telegraph and finally the war, and he is the only character who sees the ending coming — he says so, in the flattest possible terms, and is right.
characters.clue: Answers a flag of truce with a line about dismembering the messenger, to prove a point about chivalry.

characters.name: King Arthur
characters.role: The king, and later a man in peasant clothes
characters.summary: Absurd when he is on the throne and impressive the moment he is off it. Twain gives him the novel's one unqualified act of courage in the smallpox hut, and then has him sold in a slave market because he cannot stop walking like a monarch. The satire makes an exception for him, and means it.
characters.clue: Cannot learn to carry himself like a peasant, and carries a dying woman upstairs without being asked.
traits: kind in person and blind in policy

characters.name: Sandy
characters.role: Demoiselle Alisande la Carteloise, who takes the Boss on a quest
characters.summary: She talks without pausing for chapters at a time, in sentences borrowed from Malory, and the Boss treats her as a nuisance for half the book. When her castle of captive princesses turns out to be a pigsty she is unembarrassed, and by the end she has become the person he is trying to get home to.
characters.clue: Her ogres keep pigs, and she sees no difficulty in that at all.

characters.name: Merlin
characters.summary: A bore with a reputation, whose tricks stop working the moment somebody arrives with blasting powder. He spends the novel being humiliated and the last page winning: the spell that puts the Boss to sleep for thirteen centuries is the only piece of magic in the book that does what it claims.
characters.clue: Laughs, at the very end, over a sleeping man, and is killed by his own success.

characters.name: Morgan le Fay
characters.role: Arthur's sister, and the keeper of a private dungeon
characters.summary: Beautiful, gracious and casually murderous, she is the novel's clearest picture of what absolute power does to manners rather than in spite of them. Her prisoners have been forgotten so thoroughly that some of them cannot say what they were charged with.
characters.clue: Stabs a page for brushing against her knee, and goes on with the conversation.

characters.name: Sir Sagramor le Desirous
characters.role: The knight who challenges the Boss to a duel
characters.summary: He takes offence at an overheard remark in chapter nine and comes back for satisfaction years later, which is how the tournament system works. His death in the lists is the beginning of the end: it makes the Boss's methods public, and it puts the whole of chivalry on the other side.
characters.clue: Waits years for a duel and loses it to a lasso.

characters.name: Dowley
characters.role: A blacksmith in a free village
characters.summary: Prosperous, proud of his wages and unable to follow the Boss's argument about what those wages buy. Their evening together is the novel's best scene of political economy, and it ends with a lecture that terrifies its audience — not because it is wrong, but because talking like that gets men hanged.
characters.clue: Is shown that his high wages are worth less than another country's low ones, and hates being shown it.

characters.name: Hello-Central
characters.summary: Named after the only phrase of his own century he still hears, which is the novel's saddest joke. Her illness takes her parents to the coast at the moment the Church moves, so the child who exists to show that the Boss has made a life in the sixth century is also the reason he is not there to save it.
characters.clue: Her name is what a man says into a telephone when he wants to be connected.

themes.name: What a man who can make anything will make
themes.summary: Hank's gift is manufacture: guns, boilers, engines, and the machines that make them. The novel follows that gift from soap and matches through telephones to dynamite mines and Gatling guns, without ever changing its opinion that the gift is good.
themes.development: The inventions are comic for twenty chapters, useful for ten, and by the sand-belt they are a system for killing twenty-five thousand men in an afternoon with fifty-four operators.

themes.name: Kings, bosses and the habit of obedience
themes.summary: Twain's target is not one bad king but the trained reflex that makes a population accept whoever is standing above them. The Boss deplores it and then relies on it: his own power rests on exactly the awe he came to abolish.
themes.development: He takes the country with a magic trick, rules it as the Boss, and discovers at the end that the people will obey the Church's interdict the same way they obeyed him.

themes.name: The Established Church
themes.summary: The novel's stated villain is an institution rather than a faith: a church that owns the land, blesses the arrangement and can switch the nation off with an interdict.
themes.development: It is a grumble in the early chapters, a rival in the middle, and in the last five the decisive power in the book — the one force whose technology beats his.

themes.name: Freemen, serfs and wages
themes.summary: The sharpest chapters are about economics: what a wage buys, who owns the land, and why men who are being robbed defend the system that robs them. Twain gives the arguments properly, with a blacksmith who has an answer for everything except the arithmetic.
themes.development: The Boss starts by finding the serfs comic, learns to be angry on their behalf, and ends by discovering that they will march against him when told to.

themes.name: Slavery, in the sixth century and the nineteenth
themes.summary: The king and the Boss are sold as slaves and walk in a chain gang, and the novel stops being funny. Twain is writing about Britain in 528 and about the American South he grew up in, and he does not pretend otherwise.
themes.development: The theme arrives as a detail of the setting, becomes an argument in the middle chapters, and is the reason the book's comedy cannot be recovered after chapter thirty-five.

themes.name: Training, and who gets any
themes.summary: Hank's schools, his man-factory and his newspaper all rest on the belief that people are not born into their stations but taught into them. It is the novel's most generous idea and the one it tests hardest.
themes.development: The boys he trains are the only people who stand with him at the end, which proves the theory and destroys everything it was supposed to build.

themes.name: Miracles, staged
themes.summary: The eclipse, the exploding tower, the restored fountain and the electric fence are all theatre: effects produced for an audience that must not understand them. The Boss is a showman who despises the other showmen.
themes.development: Each performance is larger than the last and each requires a bigger secret, until the final effect is a battlefield and the audience is dead.

techniques.name: A manuscript handed over
techniques.definition: A story presented inside another story, with a narrator who receives rather than tells it.
techniques.inThisBook: The Warwick frame lets Twain end the book twice: once with the Boss unconscious in a cave, and once in the present with a dying man calling for a wife thirteen centuries away.

techniques.name: The wrong century in the room
techniques.definition: Placing the objects and language of one age inside another, deliberately and visibly.
techniques.inThisBook: Telephone wires in the forest, soap advertisements on knights, stove polish, a patent office in 528. The joke works in both directions: the sixth century looks absurd, and so does the nineteenth when it arrives in armour.

techniques.name: The flat report
techniques.definition: Describing something extraordinary in the tone used for routine business.
techniques.inThisBook: The account of the sand-belt is written like a works report — fences, mines, dispositions, a count of the dead. The refusal to change register is what makes the last chapters cold.

techniques.name: Scaling the joke up
techniques.definition: Exaggeration pushed until it changes what it is describing.
techniques.inThisBook: One man against a kingdom, one eclipse to win a country, one afternoon against the whole of chivalry. Twain lets the scale grow by stages so that the reader accepts the final figure of twenty-five thousand.

techniques.name: A narrator who cannot hear himself
techniques.definition: A gap between what the teller believes he is showing and what the reader sees.
techniques.inThisBook: Hank denounces men who rule by mystification while ruling by mystification, and reports his massacre as a technical success. Twain never steps in to correct him.

techniques.name: The public demonstration
techniques.definition: An extended scene staged in front of a crowd, in which the plot turns.
techniques.inThisBook: The eclipse, the blowing up of Merlin's tower, the restored fountain, the duel with Sagramor and the sand-belt are the same scene five times, each with a larger audience and a higher cost.

techniques.name: Lists of improvements
techniques.definition: Piling up items so that the accumulation itself makes the point.
techniques.inThisBook: Schools, a patent office, a newspaper, matches, soap, insurance, a stock exchange: the lists are funny, and they are also the novel showing how much of a civilisation rests on one man's memory.

quotations.text: It was in Warwick Castle that I came across the curious stranger whom I am going to talk about.
quotations.context: The first sentence of the book, spoken by the frame narrator.
quotations.analysis: A tourist's sentence, flat and unhurried, before anything strange has been allowed in. The frame is doing quiet work: it lets the impossible story arrive as somebody else's manuscript, so the reader can decide for himself what to believe.

quotations.text: So I am a Yankee of the Yankees—and practical; yes, and nearly barren of sentiment, I suppose—or poetry, in other words.
quotations.context: Hank Morgan introducing himself at the start of his manuscript.
quotations.analysis: He offers his lack of poetry as a qualification. Everything the novel goes on to test is in that boast: the man who is proud of having no sentiment will be the one deciding what a life is worth on the last afternoon.

quotations.text: Why, I could make anything a body wanted—anything in the world, it didn’t make any difference what
quotations.context: Describing his training at the arms factory in Hartford.
quotations.analysis: Stated as a workman's pride, and it is the novel's whole premise. Twain puts the emphasis on anything twice, and the second half of the book is a demonstration of what that word includes.

quotations.text: I will blot out the sun, and he shall never shine again
quotations.context: The message Hank sends to the king, timed against an eclipse he has worked out from the date.
quotations.analysis: Knowledge used as a threat, in the voice of the magicians he has been deriding. The sentence wins him the kingdom and sets the terms of his rule: he will govern by doing things nobody around him can explain.

quotations.text: the very first official thing I did, in my administration—and it was on the very first day of it, too—was to start a patent office
quotations.context: Listing the beginnings of his civilisation.
quotations.analysis: Before schools, before medicine, before food: the machinery for owning ideas. It is a joke about American priorities and a serious statement of Twain's own, made while he was bankrupting himself on a patented typesetter.

quotations.text: a country without a patent office and good patent laws was just a crab, and couldn’t travel any way but sideways or backways
quotations.analysis: The image is homely and the doctrine is absolute. Twain's habit of putting a nineteenth-century certainty into a farmyard simile is what lets the reader enjoy the opinion and doubt it at the same time.

quotations.text: Any kind of royalty, howsoever modified
quotations.context: The Boss setting out his view of hereditary rule.
quotations.analysis: The opening of the novel's plainest political statement, and it is made by a man who has just accepted the second-highest office in the kingdom. Twain lets the contradiction stand without comment for another thirty chapters.

quotations.text: unlimited power is the ideal thing when it is in safe hands
quotations.context: Hank explaining why he has not simply abolished the monarchy.
quotations.analysis: The clause that gives the book away. He means his own hands, and the novel's last chapters are the argument against the sentence — delivered not as a rebuttal but as a body count.

quotations.text: a man is a man, at bottom
quotations.context: Hank on what training does and does not reach.
quotations.analysis: The democratic premise stated in five words, and it is the belief that makes his schools worth building. The novel gives it the best evidence it has — the king in the smallpox hut — and then asks whether it survives the sand-belt.

quotations.text: I was become a stockholder in a corporation where nine hundred and ninety-four of the members furnished all the money and did all the work
quotations.context: Working out what the population of Britain actually consists of.
quotations.analysis: Twain writes social analysis as a company report: nine hundred and ninety-four workers, six shareholders. Twain's arithmetic here is the model for the economic chapters later, where the same point is made to a blacksmith who cannot bear it.

quotations.text: The blunting effects of slavery upon the slaveholder’s moral perceptions are known and conceded
quotations.context: After the king, travelling in disguise, has failed to see what is wrong with a slave gang.
quotations.analysis: Written by a man who grew up in a slaveholding town in Missouri, about a country thirteen centuries away. The sentence is careful and general, and the chapters around it are neither.

quotations.text: Fifty-four what? Men? No, minds—the capablest in the world
quotations.context: The Boss's proclamation to the massed knighthood, offering terms.
quotations.analysis: The confidence is technical and entirely justified: fifty-four trained people with electricity and machine guns can beat thirty thousand. What the sentence cannot see is that being right about this is the disaster.

quotations.text: Dismember me this animal, and return him in a basket to the base-born knave who sent him
quotations.context: Clarence acting out the answer the knights will send, to save the trouble of sending the message.
quotations.analysis: A boy performs the enemy's reply in Malory's own idiom, and is exactly right. It is the novel's best joke and its most chilling moment: the negotiation is over before it starts, and both sides know it.

quotations.text: How empty is theory in presence of fact!
quotations.analysis: He means the flag of truce. The line applies far better to everything else he has built: the schools, the newspapers and the republic have all just been shown to be theory, and the fact arriving over the hill is armed.

quotations.context: After the battle, with the dead heaped around the cave.
quotations.analysis: Four words, and the victory turns into the ending. The fifty-four cannot leave because of what they have made, and the plague that kills them comes from the men they killed — the plainest statement in Twain of what a decisive weapon does to the man holding it.

timeline.label: Twain born in Missouri
timeline.detail: In a slaveholding state, thirty years before emancipation; the slave chapters of this novel are written out of that childhood.

timeline.label: George Washington Cable gives Twain Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur
timeline.detail: George Washington Cable handed him Le Morte d'Arthur on tour, and the notebook joke about an itching knight followed within days.

timeline.label: First chapters read aloud
timeline.detail: Twain read the opening to an audience in Governor's Island and described the book as a contrast between two civilisations.

timeline.label: Twain pours money into the Paige typesetter
timeline.detail: He was pouring money into a machine of six thousand parts that never worked; the novel's faith in engineering was written by a man being ruined by it.

timeline.label: Later chapters written, including the slave gang and the sand-belt
timeline.detail: The later chapters, including the slave gang and the sand-belt, were written after the manuscript had been set aside twice.

timeline.label: First edition published by Charles L. Webster & Co.
timeline.detail: Charles L. Webster & Co. issued it in December with 220 illustrations by Dan Beard, whose drawings pushed the politics further than the text.

timeline.label: British edition published as A Yankee at the Court of King Arthur
timeline.detail: Chatto & Windus published it as A Yankee at the Court of King Arthur; English reviewers took the satire personally.

timeline.label: William Dean Howells praises the book in Harper's
timeline.detail: William Dean Howells praised the book's anger at privilege in Harper's, setting the terms for its American reception.

timeline.label: Twain's bankruptcy
timeline.detail: The typesetter failed and took his publishing house with it; he spent the next years on a lecture tour paying creditors.

timeline.label: First film version
timeline.detail: A silent adaptation began a century of screen versions that keep the eclipse and drop the sand-belt.

timeline.label: Film musical starring Bing Crosby
timeline.detail: The best-known adaptation turns the novel into a romance, which is a fair measure of how unbearable most readers find the ending.

places.name: Hartford, Connecticut
places.note: Hank's birthplace, the Colt arms factory he trained in, and the house where Twain wrote the book.

places.name: Warwick Castle
places.note: Where the frame narrator meets the stranger and is given the manuscript.

places.name: Winchester
places.note: Malory's own identification of Camelot, and as close as the novel's capital can be placed on a map.

places.name: Glastonbury
places.note: The abbey traditionally tied to Arthur's grave, and the kind of holy site the Valley of Holiness satirises.

places.name: Cadbury Castle, Somerset
places.note: The hill fort local tradition has called Camelot since the sixteenth century.

criticalViews.summary: Twain attacks hereditary rank, established religion and the sentimental medievalism of Scott and Tennyson, and gives the case for schools, wages and a free press.
criticalViews.counter: The book ends by having its democrat kill twenty-five thousand people and call it an engineering result. A satire that destroys its own spokesman is doing something other than advocacy.

criticalViews.summary: Written twenty-five years before the Western Front, the sand-belt chapters describe wire, mines, machine guns and a static killing ground with unnerving accuracy.
criticalViews.counter: Twain is extrapolating from the American Civil War rather than predicting anything, and the novel's interest is in the man behind the guns rather than in the technology.

criticalViews.position: A book that breaks in half
criticalViews.summary: The comic first half and the murderous last five chapters are often treated as two different novels, the second written by a man whose circumstances had darkened.
criticalViews.counter: The ending is prepared from chapter one: the eclipse, the tower and the fountain are all the same trick at smaller scale, and the Boss's cheerful certainty never changes.

essayQuestions.question: Is Hank Morgan the hero of this novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, irony and the man telling the story
plan: Establish his appeal: practical, funny, on the side of schools and wages and against the whip.
Collect the moments Twain lets him condemn himself, including unlimited power in safe hands.
Track the escalation of his public demonstrations from the eclipse to the sand-belt.
Weigh the smallpox hut and the slave chapters, where his anger is unquestionably the book's.
Conclude on what it means that the novel never steps outside his voice to judge him.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel use the sixth century to write about the nineteenth?
essayQuestions.focus: Satire, anachronism and the two civilisations
plan: Set out the method: Malory's Britain filled with patent offices, advertising and telephone wire.
Show the double edge — the knights look absurd, and so does the man selling them soap.
Use the slave gang, and Twain's own Missouri childhood, to argue that the target is not only the past.
Consider the Church chapters as an attack on an institution rather than a faith.
Close on the sand-belt, and what happens when the modern century arrives in full.

essayQuestions.question: What does the frame narrative achieve?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, evidence and the two endings
plan: Describe the frame: a tourist, a stranger, a palimpsest manuscript read overnight.
Note what it licenses — an impossible story told as a document rather than a claim.
Examine Clarence's postscript, and the effect of a second hand finishing the book.
Take the last page, with the dying man calling for a wife thirteen centuries away.
Argue for what would be lost if the novel simply ended in the cave.

essayQuestions.question: Does the ending follow from what comes before it?
essayQuestions.focus: Structure, escalation and the battle of the sand-belt
plan: Summarise the objection: a comic novel that ends in mass slaughter.
Trace the sequence of demonstrations, each larger and each requiring a bigger secret.
Show the Boss's tone holding steady from the eclipse to the body count.
Bring in the Interdict: the one power in the book that beats his, and why it wins.
Decide whether the ending is a collapse of control or the argument arriving on time.

discussionQuestions: Hank saves his life with an eclipse. Is that different in kind from what Merlin does?
The king carries a dying girl down from the loft in the smallpox hut. What does the novel want you to do with that scene?
Why does Twain put the patent office before the schools?
Clarence acts out the knights' answer to the flag of truce. What has he understood that the Boss has not?
Is the sand-belt a defeat or a victory, and for whom?
The book was published with illustrations that made its politics sharper. How much should a reader let pictures argue?

related.why: Twain's other book about a decent man inside a system he has been trained not to see.
Written five years later, and just as interested in what training rather than birth makes of a person.
Published six years later, and the other great scientific romance about a technology that settles an argument between two civilisations.
The tradition the Boss thinks he is joining: a visitor describing a better-arranged country.
The earlier story of a man whose great work turns on him and cannot be put back.
